_meta.schema: entry: id, tool, explain_tool?, privilege?, category, intent, rhel_versions{7,8,9,10}, flags[], verify, undo, blast, stig[], source, verified — ADR-001 §5.1
_meta.explain_tool_rule: Optional. Set only when the entry is filed under tool as the subject the operator is asking about, but every rhel_versions command actually invokes a DIFFERENT binary (e.g. firewalld-service-active is filed under firewall-cmd for navigation, but emits systemctl). When present, the inspector and the G1 gate resolve flag explanations and the tool/binary-agreement check through explain_tool instead of tool. tool still drives the sidebar Tools rail and stays the subject; explain_tool never changes what the operator sees, only which dictionary answers the flag panel (Marcus Reed Panels review PANEL-001 / condition G1).
_meta.privilege_rule: Optional, one of extract/schema.py's PRIVILEGES ("root" today). Set when the entry's OWN assembled command needs elevated privilege to run on a STIG'd host that the command text itself never requests (no sudo/su in the template) -- distinct from blast, which rates what the command DOES once it runs, not what it takes to run it. The UI shows a privilege badge next to blast and the evidence exporter records a Requires: line, so the content validation protocol's safety rule (no sudo used during a capture run) can defer the entry correctly instead of silently skipping it (G4(e); gen-sshd-test-config, sshd_config not world-readable on defiant/saratoga, CR-T-34).
_meta.status: CR-T-02 skeleton (3 curated entries) + CR-T-17..25 generator specs (24 entries): guided forms for firewall-cmd, nmcli, journalctl, lvm, sshd, useradd/usermod, systemctl, dnf/yum, semanage/setsebool, chage, auditctl/ausearch, rsyslog, chronyd, podman. Full catalog authoring is still CR-T-33.

source.title: chronyd(8) manual page, captured on the RHEL 8 extraction host (CR-T-09/10)

entries.notes: H1 correction (Marcus Reed): this entry was wrongly raised to blast yellow at G4(d) on a misreading of -Q as clock-stepping (Caleb Stone's CR-T-34 note read -Q for -q; Eli Cross's ruling and this branch's previous commit both repeated it). chronyd(8) draws a clear line between the two: -q is the mode that actually adjusts the system time and then quits (content-src/raw/rhel8/chronyd.man.txt#L64-L66, identical at rhel10#L64-L66); -Q behaves the same way except for that one adjustment -- it reports the measured offset and, because it skips opening network ports entirely, can run as a non-root user as long as nothing in the config needs elevated access (#L68-L74, identical at rhel10#L68-L74). This toolkit only ever generates -Q. blast restored to green. MCR-SEC-025: chronyd(8) SYNOPSIS is `chronyd [OPTION]... [DIRECTIVE]...` (#L7, identical at rhel10#L7), so configuration directives are OPERANDS accepted after the options, and -Q itself takes no argument (#L68). The directive is a separate word after -Q, never -Q's value. RHEL 7 uses chronyd by default for NTP (chrony package). The legacy ntpd daemon is available as an alternative from the separate ntp package but is not installed or enabled by default on any pinned release (RHEL 7 System Administrator's Guide, ch. 18-19) -- chronyd is the only NTP daemon this toolkit generates commands for.

entries.intent: See what is running on the host right now, and which process is which, before deciding what to signal

7.notes: aux shows every process for every user in the classic BSD-style columns (owner, pid, %cpu, %mem, command); the trailing ww prevents long command lines from being truncated. Reads only from /proc; changes nothing.

flags.explain: Show processes for all users, not just the caller's.
User-oriented output format: owner, %cpu, %mem, start time, etc.
Include processes with no controlling terminal (daemons).
The System V style equivalent of aux, full-format listing.
Draw the parent/child process tree with ASCII art indentation.

entries.verify: The listed process and its pid match what the operator expects to find running.
entries.undo: Nothing to undo -- read-only.

source.title: man page for ps, as installed on the reference host

entries.intent: Watch CPU and memory usage update live, per process, to find what is loading the host right now

7.notes: An interactive, continuously refreshing view (default every 3 seconds); press q to quit, k to send a signal to a process from inside top itself (which is a state change, not the read-only view), and 1 to toggle per-CPU-core detail. Without an interactive terminal, `top -b -n 1` takes one batch snapshot instead, which is the shape to use from a script.

flags.explain: Batch mode: print snapshots instead of an interactive live display, for scripts or redirection.
Number of iterations before exiting (pairs with -b for a fixed number of snapshots).
Sort by a specific column (e.g. -o %MEM).
Restrict the display to one user's processes.

entries.verify: The displayed CPU/memory figures and top consumers match what the operator expects; q exits without changing anything.
entries.undo: Nothing to undo for the view itself -- if a signal was sent from inside top with k, that follows kill's own undo (none).

source.title: man page for top, as installed on the reference host

entries.intent: Ask a process, by PID, to stop -- gracefully by default, or unconditionally with -9

7.notes: With no signal, kill sends SIGTERM, which asks the process to exit and gives it the chance to catch the signal, flush buffers, and clean up. kill -9 (SIGKILL) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored -- the kernel tears the process down immediately with no chance for it to release locks or finish writing. content/dangerous.json's dp-kill-9 pattern forces the red confirmation banner on any kill -9.

flags.explain: The default, catchable request to terminate (signal 15).
SIGKILL: unconditional, uncatchable termination -- no cleanup, no chance to ignore it.
Signal 1, traditionally used to ask a daemon to reload its configuration without restarting.
List the signal names kill understands, with their numbers.

entries.verify: `ps -p <pid>` no longer shows the process (or, for a reload signal like -HUP, the service's logs show it re-read its configuration).
entries.undo: None -- a terminated process is gone; if it was a managed service, undo means starting it again (systemctl start), not un-killing the old process instance.

source.title: man page for kill, as installed on the reference host

entries.intent: Send a signal to every process matching a name or other attribute, without looking up each PID first

7.notes: Matches against the process name by default, or the full command line with -f -- a loose pattern with -f can match more processes than intended, so a dry run with pgrep (which shares pkill's matching but only lists, never signals) is the safer first step. pkill -9 carries the same unconditional-kill risk as kill -9 and is caught by the same dp-kill-9 pattern (pkill contains the substring 'kill').

flags.explain: Match against the full command line, not just the process name -- widens the match, so check it with pgrep -f first.
SIGKILL: unconditional, uncatchable termination for every matched process.
Restrict matching to processes owned by a given user.
Require an exact match of the whole name/command line, not a substring.

entries.verify: A follow-up `pgrep` (with the same match criteria) returns nothing -- the matched processes are gone.
entries.undo: None -- terminated processes are gone; if they were managed services, undo means starting them again, not un-killing the old instances.

entries.intent: Check how much RAM and swap are in use, and how much the kernel is holding as reclaimable cache

7.notes: -h prints human-readable units. The 'available' column (not 'free') is the number that matters for 'can this host take more load' -- it already accounts for memory the kernel could reclaim from cache/buffers under pressure, which the raw 'free' column does not.

flags.explain: Human-readable sizes (K, M, G) instead of raw kilobytes.
Repeat the report every N seconds, like a lightweight top for memory only.
Force output in mebibytes.
Add a total line summing physical and swap memory.

entries.verify: The reported used/available/swap figures match what the operator expects for current load.
entries.undo: Nothing to undo -- read-only.

entries.intent: Get a one-line read on how long the host has been up and how loaded it has been over the last 1/5/15 minutes

7.notes: The three load-average numbers are 1-, 5-, and 15-minute exponentially weighted averages of the run-queue length; on their own they say nothing about WHICH process is responsible -- that's what top/ps are for. Reads only from the kernel.

flags.explain: Print only how long the system has been up, in a compact form ('up 3 days').
Print the time the system was booted, instead of the elapsed uptime.

entries.verify: The reported uptime and load figures match what the operator expects.
entries.undo: Nothing to undo -- read-only.

source.title: man page for uptime, as installed on the reference host

entries.intent: Review or edit a user's own scheduled jobs without hand-editing a spool file

7.notes: -l lists the calling user's crontab; -e opens it in $EDITOR and, on save, atomically replaces the whole crontab for that user -- there is no per-line diff or confirmation, so a typo in an untouched line survives silently unless the operator reviews the whole file before saving. -r removes a user's entire crontab outright with no prompt.

flags.explain: List the current user's crontab.
Edit the current user's crontab in $EDITOR; saving replaces the whole file.
Remove the current user's crontab entirely, with no prompt.
Operate on another user's crontab (requires privilege).

entries.verify: `crontab -l` shows the intended jobs, with the intended schedule and command, and nothing unexpected removed.
entries.undo: Restore the previous crontab from a copy taken with `crontab -l > backup.cron` before editing -- crontab -e keeps no automatic history of prior versions, and crontab -r has no undo at all.

entries.intent: See how long boot took, which unit was the critical-path bottleneck, and verify a unit file parses cleanly before enabling it

7.notes: blame lists every unit by how long it took to initialize, worst first, for finding what is slowing down boot. `systemd-analyze verify <unit>` checks a unit file for syntax and dependency problems before it is ever started -- both subcommands only read systemd's own state and files, changing nothing on the host.

flags.explain: List units by initialization time, slowest first.
Show the chain of units that determined total boot time.
Parse a unit file and report syntax/dependency problems without loading or starting it.
Print the overall boot time breakdown (firmware/loader/kernel/userspace).

entries.verify: The reported timings/verification results match what the operator expects, or verify reports the unit file as clean.
entries.undo: Nothing to undo -- read-only.
